What Apple found out about On-Policy Distillation
The Apple Research team has published a new study exploring the different gotchas of OPD (On-Policy Distillation). When it works, when it doesn't, and what mechanics are at play that contribute to its success.
Distillation from a teacher model sounds simple - just copy the teacher's signal! Right? Apple's paper reveals that teacher guidance can actively hurt a student model on tokens where it's already succeeding, and that the "best" teacher completely flips depending on the student's size and the task difficulty.
Generally to make claims like these, you'd have to train a whole frigging model first and do ablation studies. This research however proposes a cool new training-free framework that lets us directly measure OPD efficacy across a bunch of different axes! Without any training!
This article was written by me (AVB) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 inside the Paper Breakdown harness.

But first, what is On-Policy Distillation?

When training a reasoning model (like an LLM that solves math problems), one popular technique is on-policy distillation. In OPD, we have a "student" model (the model we are currently training to be better) and a "teacher" model (a more capable model that we use to guide the student's learning).
At every training step, we use this "teacher" model to provide dense, per-token supervision to a "student" model. This is what the term "distillation" means. We are trying to distill the knowledge of the larger model into the smaller model.

Btw, the teacher model can be a "more contextual" student model!
Although traditionally we saw a "teacher" as simply a "larger/capable model", this need not be true. A lot of recent methods treat the teacher simply as the student model with extra context/hints. In this scenario, we are essentially training the student model to learn the same behaviours without hints that it does when given those hints.
A stupid human example of Self-Distillation: you are struggling in a difficult exam -> you train yourself to first look up the answers online to produce answers -> then asks you to replicate your answers WITHOUT the external hints, i.e. purely from memory. In this case, you are essentially doing self-distillation where your teacher model is the cheater version of you.

Why is it called "On-Policy"?

To understand this, we need to understand how the student is trained.
  1. Pick a prompt
  2. Ask the student model to generate a rollout given the prompt. A rollout contains the probability of a token over the model's entire vocabulary at each step of the generation. If the model generated a 100-word response and the model has a vocabulary of 10K tokens, a rollout is the log-probabilities of all those 10K tokens at each generation index. Token 1: The: 10%, A: 20%, That: 50%... Token2: car: 10%, boy: 30%, man: 35%... Token3: is: 90%, are: 5%, ... Token 4: good: 50%, bad: 40%, horrible: 10% ... etc It is the full response probability space (often we only consider the sampled token instead of the full vocabulary for simplicity and resource)
  3. The teacher then supervises the student on those very rollouts. The teacher seperately generates responses on the same prompt. Assuming your teacher has the same vocabulary as your student, it also generates a bunch of tokens at each index Token 1: The: 10%, A: 50%, That: 20%... Token2: car: 10%, boy: 30%, man: 35%... Token3: is: 90%, are: 5%, ... Token 4: good: 10%, bad: 40%, horrible: 50% The teacher's response is slightly different (or way different) depending on the teacher's own capability.
  4. The teacher "supervises" by telling the student: "your distribution should look more like mine." This is done via KL Divergence losses (and more recently Reverse KL divergence loss), which penalizes the student for being different from the teacher at every token position, conditioned on the student's prior trajectory. Essentially, you bring the student's token probability distribution slightly closer to the teacher's recommendation at every training step.
So the training data, the sequences of tokens being supervised, comes from the student's own current policy. This is what makes it "on-policy." An example of "off-policy" is standard SFT (supervised finetuning), here the student is provided with pre-annotated responses from a teacher (or a ground truth dataset), and the student must simply maximize using cross-entropy loss.
Btw GRPO is on-policy coz we train the model on the student's generated responses. GRPO however, provides reward to the entire generated sequence. OPD tries to give token-by-token feedback.
SFT gives token-level feedback, but SFT is not conditioned on the student's responses. Instead we have a pre-annotated trajectory of the "best" tokens to generate and the student simply maximizes it's alignment to that. I.e. it is off-policy.
https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/on-policy-distillation/

When we use Reverse-KL, the student model becomes "mode-seeking". If the original student distribution had 0 probability of a token, it will not try to maximize the probability of that token even if the teacher rated it highly.
Think of the teacher's distribution as a landscape with two peaks (two equally valid reasoning paths):
Teacher policy has 2 peaks: 🏔️ 🏔️ Forward KL student: 🏕️ 🏕️ (spreads mass to cover both peaks) Reverse KL student: 🏔️ __ (commits hard to just one peak)
Another advantage of OPD is the reduction of exposure bias. Exposure bias is a rather legacy term you never hear about in NLP these days, I will touch on it a bit, but you can google "exposure bias and teacher forcing" to learn more. The basic gist is: because we always train the student model on it's own rollouts, it is never exposed to completely insanely different distributions ever. We are always training these models in it's own belief space. This essentially means that during inference, the model is unlikely to accidentally stumble onto a generation prefix it has never seen in training (a common thing in SFT).
There is a ton of more intuition and fine-print about how OPD works and the mechanics of Reverse-KL loss functions. Read these two articles from Will Brown (

Let's get back about Apple's paper now to understand what their study is trying to achieve.


On-Policy Distillation: Where It Helps, Where It Hurts, and Why

Apple's paper is primarily a diagnostic/analytical study, NOT a new training algorithm or a new trained model. But it does introduce a concrete new measurement framework as its core contribution.
Let's consider these questions:
  • Should the teacher be a larger external model, or the student itself with hints (self-distillation)?
  • Should the context include a full solution trace or a concise summary?
  • Does the best choice change question by question? Token by token?
Today, the only way to answer these questions is to run full expensive training runs and look at aggregate metrics - which hide what's actually happening at the individual token level.
Consider a scenario where you are training a student model on a reasoning task inside a RLVR environment. The student generates a rollout, the teacher generates another - and let's say the teacher and student disagree on a token's probability.
There are three likely reasons for this disagreement:
  1. The teacher prefers a stylistic variant (doesn't affect correctness)
  2. The teacher is redirecting toward a better reasoning path (genuinely helpful)
  3. The teacher is pushing toward a wrong continuation (actively harmful)
You cannot distinguish these three cases just by looking at the teacher's probability distribution alone. Two tokens could have the same teacher-student divergence, but one leads to a correct answer and the other doesn't in the future.
Apple's hypothesis: Any distillation algorithm that blindly minimizes KL divergence without knowing which tokens actually matter is flying blind.
Let's see what they do to diagnose this.

What They Propose: A Diagnostic Framework


The paper introduces a training-free diagnostic framework built around three key components:
1. The Generation Tree
Instead of just sampling one rollout per question, they sample many rollouts (G=200 initial rollouts per question) from the student. These share prefixes and naturally form a tree structure - each node is a token position, each edge is a next-token choice.
Basically, the model is provided a prompt, it generates 200 reasoning traces. Each reasoning trace ends with a final answer. They verify these answers and give it a success rating (correct or incorrect).
At each node, they track which tokens were chosen and whether those paths led to a correct final answer. This gives them an empirical estimate of the success probability P' - the probability of getting a correct answer after choosing token k at node u
Many common glue prefixes like "Let's think this carefully" have an equal probability of success or failure. Traces that are on the right trajectory "I need to open the door so I must find a key" will receive a high success probability because multiple future traces probably end up with a high score. Traces that are on the wrong trajectory "I need to open the door so I must find a banana" will likewise have a low score.
So far is just a model (Qwen3-0.6B) generating a bunch of rollouts and we create a massive prefix tree with their success potential at each node. So far, this has nothing to do with OPD.

2. The Ideal Gradient
With the generation tree constructed, we can now actually answer the question more statistically - does the teacher's suggested token push us towards success, or failure?
From the above tree structure, they derive a theoretical "ground truth" gradient.

The ideal per-node gradient that maximally increases the student's probability of success at each token. At each node, the ideal objective is to simply select the next tokens along the highest path or success from current node.
As simple as a Leetcode tree problem for finding maximum sum of path from current node to leaf node.
Intuitively, for any point in the generation sequence with any prefix, let's say the logit value of a token j according to the network is P(j)
  • If token j has above-average success probability → we must increase its logit
  • If token j has below-average success probability → we must decrease its logit
  • The magnitude of the update is proportional to current probability of j​ generated by the model, you only move mass you actually have.

3. The Gradient Alignment Score
Now you have everything you need to evaluate any distillation method. The gradient alignment score is simply the cosine similarity between the ideal gradient we just calculated and the gradient produced by any teacher/algorithm pair.

The key metric of the paper: the cosine similarity between the ideal gradient and the actual gradient produced by a distillation method (GKD, MiniLLM, etc.) at each node!
Crucially, this score is algorithm-agnostic. You can plug in GKD, MiniLLM, Thinking-Lab, or any future method and get a comparable number. The framework doesn't care about the training procedure - it just asks: does this gradient point the right way? Also, this generation tree is entirely agnostic of the teacher model. The generation tree is derived entirely with the student model and can be reused for all teachers.

4. Targeted Rollout Enrichment
In practice it is kinda intractable to estimate the full generation tree​ reliably at every node across a 30K-token AIME trace with a vocabulary of 150K tokens... you'd need an astronomical number of rollouts. Naively infeasible.
The paper's solution is targeted rollout enrichment: instead of sampling uniformly everywhere, they:
  1. Identify undersampled branching points: nodes where they don't yet have enough visits but have been picked in the sequence. These are high-priority nodes - the model thinks the token matters, but you don't have enough data to know if it leads to success.
  2. Construct a prefix that leads exactly to that node, then sample completions from there This gives us multiple responses with the same prefix (ending with that undersampled branching point from step 1)
  3. Each targeted rollout cascades it enriches not just the target node but all ancestors and descendants along its path simultaneously. So one rollout enriches every node along its path simultaneously. Ancestors get a free extra sample, and all descendants of the prefix also get more samples.
This cascading effect means the total budget required grows sublinearly with sequence length! You don't need linearly more rollouts just because your chain-of-thought is longer.
They also use exponentially growing depth windows: early tokens in the sequence get densely sampled (where branching is frequent and diverse), later tokens get sparser sampling (where trajectories have already committed to a direction).
Earlier in the reasoning, the model is likely to choose multiple divering reasoning paths, so they oversample there.


Experiments and Takeaways

The paper tests across a carefully chosen grid of variables:
Student models: Two sizes from the Qwen3 family:
  • Qwen3-0.6B (small, limited capacity)
  • Qwen3-1.7B (medium, more capable)
Teacher configurations: Two families:
  • Self-distillation (where the student model itself gets hints about correct answers.
  • And a larger external model (they test Qwen3 models at 4B, 8B and 14B sizes)
Datasets:
  • BoolQ — True/False reading comprehension, short reasoning chains
  • MMLU — Multiple choice knowledge questions, medium chains
  • AIME 2025 — Hard math olympiad problems, very long chains

Finding 1: Distillation Helps Most on Incorrect Paths

This is the paper's most consistent and kinda obvious finding.
The gradient alignment score is significantly higher on paths where the student got the answer wrong compared to paths where it got it right:
Why does this make sense? Think about it from first principles:
  • On an incorrect path: the student is already heading toward failure → the ideal gradient points away from the current trajectory. The teacher, who (generally) prefers success tokens, naturally pushes in the same direction → high alignment.
  • On a correct path: the student is already succeeding → the ideal gradient is weak (not much to fix). The teacher may still push the student around for stylistic reasons that don't help → low/noisy alignment.
Key implication: Blindly applying distillation on all tokens equally wastes signal - or worse, disturbs the student on paths where it was already doing well! Sometimes it is better to leave the student alone if it was already headed in the correct direction.

Finding 2: The Best Teacher Depends on Student Size

A fascinating reversal happens when you change the student model: For the small 0.6B student:
  • Self-distillation (correct-only) dominates with 2–3× higher alignment than external teachers
For the larger 1.7B student:
  • External teachers become competitive with Qwen3-8B achieves the highest alignment on BoolQ, beating all self-distillation variants
Their explanation is beautifully intuitive:
A small student (0.6B) cannot understand what a much larger external model is "saying" - the teacher's reasoning patterns are too foreign, OUTSIDE it's "belief system". But showing it a correct solution in its own reasoning style gives a targeted, comprehensible nudge. Model is so naive that the only other point of view it really understands is it's own (given hints)
For the 1.7B student, the capacity gap to an 8B teacher is smaller. The larger model's knowledge becomes understandable and exploitable.


Finding 3: What Predicts Alignment Within a Path?

The paper also asks: within a single reasoning chain, which tokens tend to have higher alignment?
  • Teacher-student divergence (KL, JS, L2 distance) correlates positively with alignment. Meaning useful signal lives where the teacher disagrees with the student
  • Distributional similarity correlates negatively. Where teacher and student agree, there's little to learn
  • BUT: all correlations are very weak (ρ≈0.02–0.04) -> no single token-level feature reliably predicts whether a teacher's nudge is helpful or harmful
  • Depth matters slightly: early tokens are templatic ("Okay, let me think..."), later tokens involve actual reasoning steps → alignment trends slightly positive with depth
More interestingly, Along a single reasoning path, the gradient alignment score oscillates between positive and negative values token by token. Meaning that even consecutive tokens on the same chain can alternate between helpful and harmful distillation signal.
You cannot just look at where the teacher disagrees and assume that's where to distill. Whether a disagreement is beneficial depends on downstream success probabilities, which you can only know by actually rolling out the model.

Finding 4: Wrong Demonstrations Hurt

Apple does more targeted experiments around self-distillation.
What type of self-distillation works? 2 methods they compare is Self-1C1W and Self-1C.
In Self-1C1W, the teacher model has access to one correct and one wront demo. And in Self-1C, the teacher has access to a correct demo. (Demo here means a reasoning trace that led to a correct/incorrect answer).
Here are the prompts for Self-1C and Self-1C1W
Including incorrect examples in the context consistently backfires:
  • Self-1C1W (correct + wrong demo) underperforms Self-1C (correct only) on both BoolQ and MMLU
  • The wrong example introduces noise rather than useful contrastive signal
  • Exception: on AIME (hard math), Self-1C1W performs better. Suggesting wrong examples may help on tasks where knowing what not to do matters more

Finding 5: Summarization Helps Larger Students

Another variant of self-distillation Apple tests on is "Self-Sum-1C"
Here, the teacher receives one of it's a correct rollouts in it's prompt but summarized by Qwen3-32B. The prompt looks like this:
  • For the 1.7B student: summarizing the demonstration (Self-Sum-1C) nearly doubles alignment (0.050 vs. 0.028 on BoolQ)
  • For the 0.6B student: summarization has mixed effects. The smaller model needs the full verbose trace to extract useful signal (Self-1C)
Again, capacity-dependent: a larger student can distill the key insight from a concise summary; a smaller one needs all the details spelled out.
The paper essentially argues that the field needs per-task, per-token diagnostic analysis before committing to any distillation recipe. Their gradient alignment framework is the a tool to achieve this. Study the full paper to understand more nuance, exact prompts they used, and different case studies across the 3 different datasets!
